title: Two New Additions to the Dementia Risk Factor List, and Two Simple Checkups That Help
seoTitle: New Dementia Risk Factors: LDL Cholesterol and Vision
description: Two new dementia risk factors, high LDL cholesterol and untreated vision loss, joined the 2024 list. See what that means and which checkups help.
featuredImageAlt: A physician reviews cholesterol lab results with an adult patient in a calm exam room
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: In 2024, researchers added high LDL cholesterol in midlife and untreated vision loss in later life to the official list of dementia risk factors we can work on. Family history is not destiny, and two simple checkups can help you start.

title: Structure Beats Willpower: What the U.S. POINTER Trial Teaches Us About Brain Health
seoTitle: U.S. POINTER Study: Why Structure May Help the Brain
description: What the U.S. POINTER study found about lifestyle and cognition, and why structure and support may help people stick with brain-healthy habits.
featuredImageAlt: A small group walks together outdoors, suggesting structured support for healthy habits
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: In the U.S. POINTER trial of 2,111 older adults at risk of cognitive decline, thinking-skill scores improved in both a self-guided and a structured lifestyle program. The structured program, with more support and accountability, was associated with a modestly larger gain.

title: Hearing and Your Brain: What the ACHIEVE Trial Found
seoTitle: Hearing and the Brain: What the ACHIEVE Trial Found
description: What the ACHIEVE trial found about hearing aids and cognition, including the 48% result in higher-risk adults and what the study did not show.
featuredImageAlt: An older adult has a hearing check with a clinician in a quiet office
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Hearing loss is one of the dementia risk factors we can work on. In the NIH-funded ACHIEVE trial, hearing care did not change cognitive decline for the full group over three years, but it was associated with about 48% slower decline in a higher-risk group.

title: You Don't Need 10,000 Steps: Walking and Your Brain
seoTitle: Walking and Brain Health: You Don't Need 10,000 Steps
description: How many steps a day are linked with brain health? A 2025 Harvard study found the association leveled off around 5,000 to 7,500 steps, not 10,000.
focusKeyword: how many steps a day for brain health
featuredImageAlt: A person walks on a neighborhood path in soft morning light, wearing comfortable shoes
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: A 2025 Harvard Aging Brain Study paper found that, in cognitively healthy older adults with elevated amyloid, higher daily step counts were associated with slower tau buildup and slower cognitive decline. The link leveled off around 5,000 to 7,500 steps a day.

title: Brain Fog or Something More? Telling Everyday Slips From Changes Worth a Conversation
seoTitle: Brain Fog or Dementia? Everyday Slips vs. Warning Signs
description: Is it brain fog or something more? How to tell everyday memory slips from changes worth a doctor visit, using the Alzheimer's Association warning signs.
featuredImageAlt: A person pauses in a doorway, looking thoughtful, in a quietly lit home
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Walking into a room and forgetting why is common at any age. So is feeling foggy after poor sleep, stress, or illness. Here is a calm way to tell everyday slips from changes that are worth a conversation with your doctor.

title: Sleep Is Brain Maintenance: What We Know, and Don't, About Sleep and Alzheimer's
seoTitle: Sleep and Alzheimer's: What We Know and Don't Know
description: What science says about sleep and Alzheimer's risk, including what we don't know yet, plus the 7 to 9 hour goal and when to ask about apnea.
featuredImageAlt: A peaceful bedroom in evening light, with a made bed and a lamp turned low
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Poor sleep and sleep-disordered breathing are associated with cognitive decline, and the link with Alzheimer's appears to run in both directions. It is not yet known whether improving sleep lowers Alzheimer's risk, but 7 to 9 hours and good sleep habits are still a sound investment.

title: A Brain-Friendly Thanksgiving Plate: The MIND Diet, Honestly
seoTitle: The MIND Diet at Thanksgiving: An Honest Look
description: What the MIND diet trial really found, and how to build a brain-friendly Thanksgiving plate with greens, berries, nuts, olive oil, and fish.
featuredImageAlt: A holiday table with a colorful plate of greens, roasted vegetables, berries, nuts, and fish
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: The MIND diet has encouraging long-term observational research, but in a 2023 three-year trial, both the MIND group and the control group improved, with no significant difference between them. Here is an honest take, plus simple ways to fill a holiday plate with greens, berries, nuts, olive oil, and fish.

title: Connection Is Brain Care: Staying Close Through the Holidays
seoTitle: Social Connection and Brain Health Through the Holidays
description: Why social connection is part of brain care, what research says about loneliness and cognition, and NIA-backed ways to stay close through the holidays.
featuredImageAlt: Two people share a warm conversation over coffee at a kitchen table
author: Lori King, MD
excerpt: Social isolation and loneliness are associated with higher risk of cognitive decline, Alzheimer's disease, depression, and heart disease. Connection is one of the dementia risk factors we can work on, and the holidays are a natural time to practice it, without guilt.
